tasks.name: Use pointer relationships to eliminate or compact candidates

concepts.name: Opposing two pointers
concepts.description: Use ordered structure to move left/right boundaries and discard groups of impossible candidates without checking every pair.

concepts.name: Read/write pointers
concepts.description: Scan input with one pointer while another marks where the next accepted or compacted item should be written.

concepts.name: Fast/slow pointer relationship
concepts.description: Maintain two traversals with different rates or a fixed gap to detect cycles, midpoints, or relative-position properties.

concepts.name: Fixed sliding window
concepts.description: Maintain state for one contiguous region of constant size by adding the entering item and removing the leaving item.

concepts.name: Variable sliding window
concepts.description: Expand one boundary and move the other only as needed to restore a validity condition that supports monotonic repair.

concepts.name: Window pattern discrimination
concepts.description: Distinguish moving-window problems from prefix-state queries and other range methods based on contiguity, overlap, and whether validity can be repaired by boundary movement.

concepts.name: Sort and merge intervals
concepts.description: Sort ranges by a boundary so overlap with the current merged frontier can be decided in one scan.

concepts.name: Interval endpoint semantics
concepts.description: Treat open, closed, and half-open endpoints according to the contract because endpoint-touching may or may not count as overlap.

questions.prompt: Implement `sorted_two_sum_indices(values, target)`. `values` is sorted ascending. Return `[left_index, right_index]` for a pair that sums to `target`, or `[]` if none exists. Use O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: Repair `max_window_sum`. The current code adds each entering value but forgets to remove the value that leaves the fixed-size window.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.

interaction.starter_code:
def max_window_sum(values, k):
    total = sum(values[:k])
    best = total

    for right in range(k, len(values)):
        total += values[right]
        best = max(best, total)

    return best

questions.explanation: After the new value enters, subtract `values[right-k]` so `total` still represents exactly `k` elements.
hints: Ask which old index just left the window.
The window size must remain exactly `k`.

questions.prompt: Complete `window_sums(values, k)`. Return the sum of every contiguous window of exactly `k` values, from left to right. Example: `window_sums([4, 2, 7, 1], 3) -> [13, 10]`: the first window is `[4,2,7]`; when the window moves right, `1` enters and `4` leaves. In the loop, `right` is the index of the NEW value entering the window. The element exactly `k` positions behind `right` is the one leaving. Fill those two expressions so `total` always represents exactly k elements.
questions.explanation: The new right value enters, and the value exactly `k` positions behind it leaves.
hints: The entering element is at the current right index.
The leaving element is k indexes behind the entering element.

questions.explanation: Sort by start, then compare each interval with the current merged interval. For closed intervals, `next_start <= current_end` means overlap.

questions.prompt: Complete the overlap comparisons for two interval conventions. Example: for CLOSED intervals `[start, end]`, both endpoints are included, so `[1, 3]` and `[3, 5]` overlap at value 3. For HALF-OPEN intervals `[start, end)`, the end is excluded, so `[1, 3)` and `[3, 5)` only touch and do NOT overlap. `current_end` is the end of the current merged interval and `next_start` is the next interval's start. Fill the comparison operator for each convention.
questions.explanation: Closed intervals share an endpoint, so equality counts as overlap. Half-open intervals exclude the end, so touching at equality does not overlap.
hints: Closed intervals count equality at the boundary as overlap.
Half-open intervals require the next start to be strictly before the current end.
